entries.title: Active Directory credentials dumped via DCSync/SAM ({count} accounts)
entries.description: secretsdump.py extracted NTLM password hashes from the target domain controller via DCSync (replicating AD replication protocol) or direct SAM database access. These hashes allow offline cracking or immediate pass-the-hash lateral movement without knowing the plaintext password.
entries.impact: An attacker with these hashes can impersonate any dumped account, including domain administrators, via pass-the-hash attacks. This grants full domain compromise: lateral movement to any domain-joined host, access to all domain resources, persistence via golden/silver ticket forging, and extraction of all sensitive data stored in Active Directory.

mitre_attack.name: OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager

entries.remediation_brief: Restrict DCSync-capable permissions (Replicating Directory Changes) to only Domain Controllers. Enable LSA Protection (RunAsPPL). Rotate the krbtgt account password twice to invalidate golden tickets. Implement tiered administration to limit privileged account exposure.

entries.title: Service tickets captured for Kerberoasting ({count} hash(es))
entries.description: GetUserSPNs.py requested TGS service tickets for accounts with Service Principal Names (SPNs). The resulting TGS-REP hashes are encrypted with the service account's NTLM hash and can be cracked offline to recover plaintext passwords without generating authentication failures.
entries.impact: An attacker who cracks these service account passwords gains access to every resource the service account can reach. Service accounts frequently have elevated privileges (database access, admin group membership, delegation rights) and their passwords are rarely rotated, making this a high-value lateral movement path.

mitre_attack.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting

entries.remediation_brief: Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) with automatically rotated 240+ character passwords. For accounts that cannot use gMSAs, enforce 30+ character random passwords and rotate them quarterly. Remove unnecessary SPNs from user accounts.

entries.title: AS-REP roastable accounts found ({count} hash(es))
entries.description: GetNPUsers.py identified accounts with the DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag set. AS-REP hashes for these accounts were captured without any authentication, and can be cracked offline to recover plaintext passwords.
entries.impact: An attacker can obtain crackable hashes for these accounts without valid credentials — only network access to the DC is needed. Once cracked, the compromised accounts provide authenticated domain access for further enumeration, lateral movement, and privilege escalation.

mitre_attack.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: AS-REP Roasting

entries.remediation_brief: Disable the DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag on all accounts. Audit accounts regularly for this flag via PowerShell: Get-ADUser -Filter {DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true}. Enforce strong passwords on any account that must retain this setting.

entries.title: SMB signing not required on {target}
entries.description: The target host does not require SMB message signing. This makes it vulnerable to man-in-the-middle NTLM relay attacks where an attacker intercepts authentication attempts and relays them to this host.
entries.impact: An attacker positioned on the network can relay captured NTLM authentication from any user (including administrators) to this host, gaining authenticated access without knowing credentials. Combined with LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning (captured by tools like Responder), this enables unauthenticated remote code execution on the target.

mitre_attack.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay

entries.remediation_brief: Enable SMB signing via Group Policy: set 'Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)' to Enabled. Apply to all domain-joined hosts. For domain controllers, this is the default and should not be changed.

entries.title: Domain users enumerated via LDAP ({count} accounts)
entries.description: GetADUsers.py enumerated domain user accounts via LDAP queries against the domain controller. This provides a complete inventory of Active Directory users, including their attributes, last logon times, and account status.
entries.impact: A domain user list enables targeted attacks: password spraying against known accounts, social engineering using real names and email addresses, and identification of service accounts, dormant accounts, and privileged users for further exploitation.
entries.remediation_brief: Restrict anonymous LDAP access. Implement LDAP signing and channel binding. Review which accounts have broad LDAP read permissions and reduce them to least privilege.

entries.title: Domain users enumerated via SID brute-force ({count} accounts)
entries.description: lookupsid.py brute-forced Security Identifier (SID) values to enumerate domain users and groups. This technique works even when LDAP anonymous access is restricted because it queries the LSA RPC interface.
entries.impact: Provides an alternative user enumeration path when LDAP is locked down. The resulting user list enables password spraying and targeted social engineering. Also reveals group memberships and domain SID, useful for crafting golden/silver tickets.
entries.remediation_brief: Restrict anonymous access to the SAM and LSA via Group Policy: 'Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares'. Configure RestrictAnonymousSAM registry key.

entries.title: Weak password policy: minimum length {min_length} characters
entries.description: samrdump.py retrieved the domain password policy via the SAM Remote Interface and identified weak settings: insufficient minimum password length (below 14 characters) or missing account lockout threshold (allowing unlimited brute-force attempts).
entries.impact: A weak password policy directly enables password attacks. Without adequate length requirements, accounts are vulnerable to dictionary and brute-force attacks. Without lockout thresholds, an attacker can make unlimited login attempts without triggering account lockout or alerts.
entries.remediation_brief: Set minimum password length to 14+ characters. Configure account lockout threshold to 5-10 attempts. Enable password complexity requirements. Consider implementing Azure AD Password Protection for banned password lists.

entries.title: Kerberos delegation misconfiguration ({type})
entries.description: findDelegation.py identified accounts with Kerberos delegation configured. Unconstrained delegation allows the account to impersonate any user to any service. Constrained delegation limits impersonation to specified services. Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) can be abused for privilege escalation if write access to the attribute is granted to a compromised account.
entries.impact: Unconstrained delegation: full domain compromise if the delegating account is compromised, since any user's TGT is cached. Constrained delegation: access to the specific target services as any user. RBCD: privilege escalation from any account with write access to msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity.

mitre_attack.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket

entries.remediation_brief: Remove unconstrained delegation from all accounts except Domain Controllers. Use constrained delegation with protocol transition only where necessary. Audit RBCD configurations and restrict write access to the msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute.

entries.title: Service Principal Names enumerated ({count} SPN(s))
entries.description: GetUserSPNs.py (list mode, no ticket request) enumerated all Service Principal Names registered in the domain. This provides an inventory of service accounts that are potential Kerberoasting targets.
entries.impact: The SPN inventory reveals all service accounts and the services they run. Each SPN is a Kerberoasting target — an attacker can request a service ticket for any of them and attempt offline cracking. The list also reveals the infrastructure topology (SQL servers, web servers, exchange, etc.).
entries.remediation_brief: Remove unnecessary SPNs from user accounts. Migrate service accounts to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs). Enforce strong (30+ character) passwords on remaining SPN-bearing accounts.

entries.title: Pass-the-Hash remote execution validated on {target}
entries.description: Remote code execution was validated on the target using captured NTLM hashes via wmiexec.py, psexec.py, or smbexec.py. The tool tried wmiexec first (stealthiest — no service creation, no disk writes), falling back through psexec (creates a service binary) and smbexec (creates a batch file) if needed.
entries.impact: An attacker with captured NTLM hashes can execute arbitrary commands on the target host as the hash owner. If the hash belongs to a local administrator or domain admin, this grants full control of the host: command execution, file access, credential dumping, persistence installation, and lateral movement to other hosts.

mitre_attack.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash

entries.remediation_brief: Disable local administrator hash reuse via 'Deny access to this computer from the network' for the local admin account. Deploy LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) to randomize local admin passwords. Enable Credential Guard on Windows 10+ endpoints. Implement tiered administration to limit hash exposure.

entries.title: DCOM remote execution validated on {target}
entries.description: dcomexec.py validated remote code execution via Distributed COM (DCOM) on the target host. DCOM execution uses the MMC20.Application or ShellWindows COM objects to spawn processes remotely, often evading detection rules that monitor SMB-based execution.
entries.impact: An attacker can execute arbitrary commands on the target via DCOM, which operates over RPC (port 135 + high ports) rather than SMB. This lateral movement path bypasses SMB-focused detection and does not require SMB signing. Combined with captured credentials or hashes, it provides full remote control of the target.

mitre_attack.name: Remote Services: Distributed Component Object Model
Component Object Model and Distributed COM

entries.remediation_brief: Disable remote DCOM access where not required. Restrict DCOM permissions via dcomcnfg.exe — remove non-admin users from launch and activation permissions. Block RPC high ports between workstations (firewall segmentation). Monitor Event ID 4688 for suspicious process creation via DCOM.

entries.title: TGT obtained for {user}@{domain} from {target}
entries.description: getTGT.py successfully obtained a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) from the domain controller using captured credentials. The TGT was saved as a ccache file and proves the credentials are valid for Kerberos authentication against the domain.
entries.impact: A valid TGT grants the holder authenticated access to any Kerberos-enabled service in the domain. It enables lateral movement via Kerberos (without revealing the password to remote hosts), service ticket requests for any SPN, and further exploitation of delegation relationships. The TGT is evidence of successful credential compromise.

mitre_attack.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting

entries.remediation_brief: Immediately reset the compromised account's password. Review how the credential was obtained and remediate the root cause. Enable MFA for the affected account. Monitor for anomalous Kerberos ticket requests (Event ID 4768).

entries.title: Service ticket obtained for SPN {spn} from {target}
entries.description: getST.py successfully obtained a Kerberos service ticket (TGS) for a specific Service Principal Name. This proves the captured credentials can access the target service and the ticket can be used for authentication without re-presenting the password.
entries.impact: A valid service ticket allows the holder to authenticate to the target service as the impersonated user. Depending on the SPN, this could grant access to databases (MSSQLSvc), web applications (HTTP), file shares (CIFS), or remote administration (HOST/WSMAN). The ticket can also be cracked offline if the service account has a weak password.

mitre_attack.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting

entries.remediation_brief: Reset the compromised account's password. Rotate the target service account's password (use a gMSA if possible). Review and restrict SPN assignments. Monitor Event ID 4769 for anomalous service ticket requests.

entries.title: Authenticated share access on {target} ({share_count} shares)
entries.description: Authenticated SMB share enumeration via smbclient.py discovered accessible shares on the target host. This goes beyond null-session enumeration (SS3) by using valid domain credentials to enumerate shares that require authentication, including checking read/write access to administrative shares (ADMIN$, C$, IPC$).
entries.impact: Readable non-default shares may expose sensitive data (configuration files, scripts, backup databases). Writable shares enable malware deployment and persistence. Write access to ADMIN$ or C$ proves local administrator privileges and enables remote code execution via service creation or file overwrite attacks.
entries.remediation_brief: Remove unnecessary shares. Restrict ADMIN$ and C$ access to Domain Admins only (disable remote admin share access for non-admin accounts via registry). Apply least-privilege NTFS and share permissions. Audit share permissions regularly with PowerShell: Get-SmbShare | Get-SmbShareAccess.

entries.title: Auto-logon credentials found in registry on {target}
entries.description: reg.py remotely read the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon registry key and found auto-logon credentials (DefaultUserName + DefaultPassword stored in cleartext). These credentials are stored unencrypted in the registry for automatic login purposes.
entries.impact: Auto-logon credentials are stored in plaintext and readable by any authenticated user with remote registry access. If the auto-logon account has elevated privileges (administrator, service account), compromise of these credentials enables immediate privilege escalation and lateral movement.
entries.remediation_brief: Remove auto-logon credentials from the registry: delete DefaultPassword from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon. If auto-logon is required, use Autologon.exe from Sysinternals which encrypts the password with LSA secrets. Restrict remote registry access.

entries.title: GPP cpassword found in SYSVOL on {target}
entries.description: Group Policy Preferences XML files in SYSVOL contain encrypted passwords (cpassword attribute). The AES-256 encryption key was published by Microsoft in 2012 (MS14-025), making every cpassword trivially decryptable. The tool extracted and decrypted these credentials from Groups.xml, Services.xml, Scheduledtasks.xml, DataSources.xml, Printers.xml, and Drives.xml files.
entries.impact: GPP passwords are typically set by administrators for local admin accounts, service accounts, or mapped drive credentials. Decrypting them instantly reveals plaintext credentials that may still be active. If the GPP-set password applies to a local administrator account across multiple machines (common pattern), a single GPP password compromise grants admin access to every affected host.
entries.remediation_brief: Delete all GPP XML files containing cpassword from SYSVOL immediately. Install KB2962486 (MS14-025) on all domain controllers to prevent creation of new GPP passwords. Reset all passwords that were stored in GPP. Deploy LAPS for local administrator password management instead.

entries.title: NTLM relay attack {result} against {target}
entries.description: ntlmrelayx.py was used to validate that NTLM relay attacks are exploitable against the target host. The host does not require SMB signing, allowing intercepted NTLM authentication to be relayed and accepted without modification.
entries.impact: An attacker positioned on the network can relay captured NTLM authentication from any user — including domain administrators — to this host. Combined with LLMNR/NBT-NS/WPAD poisoning, this enables unauthenticated remote code execution. A single relay of a privileged account can lead to full domain compromise.

mitre_attack.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay

entries.remediation_brief: Enable SMB signing on all domain-joined hosts via Group Policy ('Digitally sign communications (always)'). Disable NTLM authentication where possible via 'Network security: Restrict NTLM' policies. Enable EPA (Extended Protection for Authentication) on all web services. Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS via GPO.

entries.title: Valid credentials discovered via password spray ({count} account(s))
entries.description: getTGT.py was used to perform a controlled password spray against domain accounts. One or more accounts accepted a guessed password, proving that weak or commonly-used passwords are in active use in the domain.
entries.impact: Compromised domain credentials provide authenticated access for enumeration, lateral movement, and privilege escalation. If the sprayed account has elevated privileges (helpdesk, service account, admin), the impact escalates to potential domain compromise. Even a standard user account enables internal reconnaissance and Kerberoasting.
entries.remediation_brief: Enforce 14+ character minimum password length via Group Policy. Deploy Azure AD Password Protection or a similar banned-password list to block common passwords. Configure account lockout (5-10 attempts, 30-minute lockout). Implement MFA for all domain accounts. Monitor Event ID 4771 for Kerberos pre-authentication failures.

entries.title: DPAPI domain backup key extracted from {target}
entries.description: dpapi.py backupkeys retrieved the domain DPAPI backup key from the domain controller. This key is used to encrypt DPAPI master keys for all domain users, allowing decryption of any DPAPI-protected secret on any domain-joined machine.
entries.impact: With the DPAPI backup key, an attacker can decrypt any credential protected by Windows Data Protection API on any domain-joined machine: saved browser passwords, RDP credentials, Wi-Fi keys, EFS-encrypted files, certificate private keys, and application secrets. This is a domain-wide secret-recovery capability that persists until the backup key is rotated.

mitre_attack.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers

entries.remediation_brief: Rotate the DPAPI domain backup key (requires domain functional level 2012 R2+). Restrict access to the ms-Bkrp-BackupKey attribute to Domain Controllers only. Monitor Event ID 4662 for backup key access. Limit the number of Domain Admin accounts. Consider Credential Guard on sensitive hosts.
